title: Rulin Shao (@RulinShao) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Introduce LightSeq for long-context LLM training:
- Highly optimized for decoder models
- smarter checkpointing
- better support for fewer heads models
up to 2x faster, 2-8x longer sequences vs Megatron-LM.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/F8GqQaHbMAAfpWK.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/F8GqQaHbMAAfpWK.mp4
────────
[2/8] Our design also enables overlapping communication with computation. Experimental results show that substantial communication can be hidden in LightSeq.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8Gk7Era0AAwWVQ.jpg
────────
[3/8] We note that the workload in LLMs is imbalanced as the later tokens have a longer context to attend to, causing computation bubbles in sequence parallelism. To fix it, we designed a load-balancing algorithm letting the bubble workers help the busy workers.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8GkHI4agAAOeDO.jpg
────────
[4/8] LightSeq features distributed attention (DistAttn). It splits the input seq into chunks and distributes the computation of each chunk to one GPU. All modules but attention are embarrassingly parallelized. DistAttn communicates keys and values to complete the computation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8GpE5Ua4AA-_N5.jpg
────────
[5/8] Our experiments show that LightSeq has faster training speed and better support for LLMs with different heads than Megatron-LM on both intra- and inter-node training with NVLINK and Infiniband.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8GmoEXaEAApHqJ.jpg
────────
[6/8] When developing DistAttn, we discovered a better grad checkpointing strategy in the presence of
FlashAttention (FA). This is because FA does rematerialization inside its backward kernel, which makes recomputation redundant. More interestingly, this applies to any cases with FA.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8GmAQoa0AAULdT.jpg
────────
[7/8] The paper is on:
Code preview: We're preparing to release end-to-end training code soon.
The work is done by amazing collaborators @DachengLi177, @RulinShao, Anze Xie, @ericxing, @profjoeyg, Ion Stoica, @MaxMa1987, @haozhangml
────────
[8/8] LightSeq solely uses sequence parallelism and thus doesn’t pose any assumptions on the model architecture like the number of heads. Therefore, LightSeq can scale beyond the number of heads and easily handle models with only a few attention heads.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8Gmso8bMAAS4ks.png

Our evolving rubrics
- Generated by comparing rollouts during training
- Conditioned on searched knowledge
- Select the rubrics with the highest reward std when evolving

────────

- Questions are under-specified 🥹
- Require massive knowledge to evaluate 😱
We present the first training recipe for long-form DR! 😎

DR Tulu-8B:

I've been far wishing to have an online serving version of MassiveDS since its release in 2024. Here's a roadmap that I've witnessed with wonderful mentors @sewon__min @Tim_Dettmers :
1. We initially developed a CPU-based serving code that performs distributed search for MassiveDS. This code has been used in some Meta and AI2 projects, but it was painful to monitor the jobs that we needed to relaunch the server frequently and grab unnecessarily expensive nodes for serving.
2. Another aspect is the data quality. It was unclear how to filter high-quality data for a retrieval datastore to cut costs. This problem was explored in CompactDS led by @XinxiLyu & @micdun8, advised by @sewon__min. They did a scary amount of careful ablations on how data composition, vector compression, and reranking can impact model performance. As a result, they built CompactDS that, as its name indicates, is a higher-quality version of MassiveDS.
3. Despite CompactDS made it possible to serve one giant index on one node with 1TB CPU memory, the latency and throughput were still not satisfying. @YichuanM and @jinjianliuu, as the experts of efficient IR system, built this DS-Serve that finally made the large-scale index usable in online serving applications. Rulin Shao presents Context Language Models (CLMs), which treat context management as a skill learned within the model itself rather than relying on external harnesses. CLMs manage their context as an editable file, allowing flexible manipulation and coexistence of multiple contexts in multi-agent setups. This approach outperforms existing methods like Codex summary and OpenEvolve on tasks including long-term reasoning and coding, while reducing costs.

CLMs can improve further through online reinforcement learning, gaining efficiency and accuracy. They also allow direct steering and evolution via in-context textual changes. To handle the computational cost of arbitrary context edits, Shao introduces Prefix-Reuse FLOPs and a Suffix Cache Reuse method, maintaining efficiency. Alongside CLMs, Shao offers ContextBench, a benchmark to evaluate context management abilities, and provides open code and tools for experimentation.

title: Rulin Shao (@RulinShao)
summary:
CLM is one of the most elegant ideas we've worked on together.
To me, it starts with a simple interaction need: there are many cases where I just want the agent to make surgical edits to the context. For example, when the agent finishes one task and prepares for another, it should ideally be able to clean up the context for the next one, just as a human would. And there are many such cases!
Instead of hard-coding such rules into the harness (I doubt that's even possible), what would a first-principles solution to this problem look like? It turns out to be shockingly simple: ask the LLM to manage the context itself! Not only can this help the agent more efficiently solve the next task, but it can also be applied recursively to many more complex cases.
This unlocks new agent capabilities across a variety of challenging, long-running, and open-ended tasks. For example, equipped with CLM, the agents can run continuously for hours on challenging tasks like EdgeBench or our new software world repository optimization tasks, and achieve really good results. Check out the CLM paper for more method details and many other cool results!

summary:
[1/2] More details on how we implemented Suffix Cache Reuse for hybrid attention (interleaved full and linear attention layers) based on @sgl_project are provided in the appendix. We also provide (1) Detailed decomposition of cache hit rate wrt CLM context editing and reasoning token stripping, and (2) remaining space for future improvement of cache hit rate. We see CACHE space as a promising direction to play around that *you can do more fancy manipulations in the cache space beside token space*! We will drop a more readable blog about it soon😌
Quoting @RulinShao
@billxbf @shannonzshen @oscar_yinn @yuetai12575 @hamishivi @natolambert @TengX6 @ml_perception @scottyih @LukeZettlemoyer @PangWeiKoh Hi Binfeng, thanks for your nice words! Regarding KV cache, our efficiency metric (prefix reuse FLOPs) accounted for the reprefilling cost induced by un-hit KV cache. So when we say CLMs are cheaper it means cheaper with lower hit rate.
As for the accurate profiling, we did have analysis, and we also proposed a further fix for it. As you can see from this figure for BCP, the hit rate for edited turns are lower than normal turns (73.9->29.9). What we proposed is to instead throwing away the cache for unmatched suffix, we reuse them as well. Then it added 28.2% more hit rate for edited turns. The total prefix-reuse FLOPs dropped from 10.98/Q to 7.14/Q with matched performance. Note that CLMs were already more efficient than existing baselines with standard serving through better context management, and this further reduced the serving cost to 65%.
There are other factors that can also impact KV cache hit rate, such as some chat templates strip thinking tokens away in future turns, causing each turn's final output being reprefilled twice. We find our SCR can also hit that cache. The second screenshot shows a decomposition of the cache we hit--surprisingly, the reasoning cache was more than the CLM edits cache.
If you'd like to look into it deeper, please checkout the third figure: we also studied why there are still some unhit cache, and we found the standard SGLang isn't doing perfectly on this hybrid attention architecture, because for linear attention, there's only state snapshots being captured every a block of tokens, not per-token cache like in full attention layers. So we found there's 8.1% of prefix-matched cache being missed by standard SGLang among all turns (29.5% in edited turns), similarly SCR also has a similar margin for future improvement (maybe with more frequent snapshots trading off memory, or better techniques for it). I think there can be many good future research directions in this space!
(Due to space limit, we move most of the details for SRC in the appendix B. Feel free to check it out!)

clean_summary:
Suffix Cache Reuse (SCR) tackles the problem of low key-value (KV) cache hit rates in hybrid attention models that combine full and linear attention layers. Low hit rates mean the model must recompute many tokens, increasing cost. SCR reuses unmatched suffixes in the cache instead of discarding them, boosting hit rates especially in edited contexts where hits dropped from 73.9% to 29.9%.

This reuse cut the required computations (prefix-reuse FLOPs) from 10.98 to 7.14 per query, reducing serving cost to 65% of previous levels without losing performance. SCR also captures reasoning tokens often stripped by chat templates. Some cache misses remain due to linear attention's less frequent state snapshots, suggesting future improvements. The SCR code and detailed analysis are available in the Facebook research repository.

clean_title: Self-managed context skill for agents to edit their working memory
summary:
Wow this is such a cool skill for visualizing how CLMs work! 🤩 Thanks for making and sharing it!
Quoting @muratcan
New skill: self-managed-context
(make the agent's context an editable file)
It explains how to build agents that decide what to keep, update, or remove from the information they use to do their work. It can archive a long log while keeping the exact error, update its progress notes, or remove outdated information. Those edits then change what the model sees on its next turn.
1- Keep the system instructions and original task protected, outside the editable file.
2- Write the remaining conversation to a file, with labels for each message.
3- Let the agent edit that file using its usual code tools.
4- After each command, read the file back and use the updated messages for the next model call.
Loading the skill ( alone into a fixed harness won't create live context editing, but it can help an agent build and then operate a harness that supports it.
I gave the skill to a coding agent and had it build the harness itself.
The task is a long stream of server logs that doesn't fit in the window. The agent reads it in 18 chunks, about 10k tokens in total, with a 5.5k budget. It has to report one incident ticket exactly and the final value of every config key.
Same model & budget, three setups:
1- Model manages its own context
2- Harness forces a summary at 75% full
3- Keeps everything
The video shows a real GPT-5.4 run.
- Self-managed solved it 3 out of 3.
- Keep-everything overflowed 3 out of 3.
- Forced summary also solved it 3 out of 3.
On GPT-5.4 the self-managed agent re-processed about 24% fewer prompt tokens than the forced summary. When it edited, it cut hard, so little was left after the edit to re-process (one edit took 5,537 tokens down to 771).
On GPT-4.1 it saved nothing. It edited near the top of its context but kept most of what was below, and every edit forces everything after it to be re-processed.
This is a small test at about 2x context pressure. The paper goes up to 24x, but imho the video below and the skill are a good way to start understanding the technique.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2105792293441511424/img/QKfDORSB3n_cMJlm.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2105792293441511424/vid/avc1/480x270/0A63ltgOc47XASJA.mp4?tag=29
clean_summary:
When agents handle long tasks, their context window can overflow, forcing them to summarize or drop information. This usually wastes tokens or loses details. The challenge is to keep the right info while staying within token limits.

Muratcan’s self-managed-context skill lets an agent keep its context in an editable file. The agent decides what to keep, update, or remove, editing the file between turns. This way, it can archive logs, update notes, or remove outdated info, changing what it sees next. On GPT-5.4, this saved about 24% of tokens compared to forced summaries, solving all test cases with less re-processing. Federico Shao calls it a cool way to visualize how causal language models manage their context.

You might think reasoning in language models comes mainly from reinforcement learning, but Rulin Shao highlights a new explanation focused on the training data itself. The idea is that certain early tokens in a prompt act like routers, guiding the model to relevant knowledge learned during mid-training. This is similar to how mixture-of-experts models work, where different parts of the model activate for different inputs.

summary:
Frontier LLMs are good at individual tasks, but real-world long-horizon reasoning isn't about isolated skills. 🚨 It is about switching between skills‼️
Our new paper introduces ✨Skill Entropy✨, a principled measure of how hard it is to switch from one reasoning skill to another. Our key observation:
👉 Even if an LLM masters individual skills, it still often FAILS at skill switching.
We use this signal for both benchmarking AND training:
🤹We introduce Skill²-Bench, built over 558 skills across 9 domains. Accuracy of 8 frontier and 4 open thinking models DROPS nearly monotonically as skill-switching difficulty rises.
🔗 Paper:
💻 Code:
🏋️ We further implement Skill-Entropy RL, which grades the model on its skill-switching competence. Our method beats competitive skill-aware baselines by >7% on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-1.7B.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPBUf99bMAA7Tt6.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPBUmEobkAE82A3.jpg
clean_summary:
Frontier large language models (LLMs) handle individual tasks well, but real-world problems require switching between different reasoning skills over long horizons. Rulin Shao points out that even when LLMs master single skills, they often fail at switching between them.

To address this, they introduce Skill Entropy, a measure of how hard it is to switch from one skill to another. They build Skill²-Bench with 558 skills across 9 domains, showing accuracy drops as skill-switching difficulty rises. They also propose Skill-Entropy RL, a training method that improves skill-switching competence, outperforming other skill-aware baselines by over 7% on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-1.7B models.
